name: Xiriâna
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Ramirez, Henri 1992. Bahuana: une nouvelle langue de la famille Arawak (Amerindia grammar); no online copy found.

new_statements.quote: 3. l'accent tonique tombe en général sur l'avant-dernière syllabe du mot, et, très souvent, il implique l'allongement de la voyelle accentuée : nahɨ [na:hə] 'ma dent'. L'accent secondaire tombe deux syllabes avant l'accent primaire. [p. 26:] Les exceptions à la règle sont rares : kiba [ki:ba] 'montagne', kibada [ki:bada] 'pierre'. [...] L'accent touche le mot en sa totalité, quels que soient les affixes associés [...] Les mots qui se terminent par une occlusion glottale (perte de voyelle en style rapide) sont accentués sur la dernière syllabe [...] Nous n'avons pas trouvé de paires de morphèmes où l'accent ait une valeur distinctive.
new_statements.translation: 3. The tonic accent falls in general on the penultimate syllable of the word, and very often it entails lengthening of the stressed vowel: nahɨ [na:hə] 'my tooth'. Secondary stress falls two syllables before the primary stress. [p. 26:] Exceptions to the rule are rare: kiba [ki:ba] 'mountain', kibada [ki:bada] 'stone'. [...] Stress applies to the word as a whole, whatever affixes are attached [...] Words ending in a glottal stop (loss of a vowel in rapid speech) are stressed on the last syllable [...] We have found no pairs of morphemes in which stress has a distinctive value.
new_statements.citation: Ramirez, Henri. 1992. Le Bahuana: une nouvelle langue de la famille arawak. Supplément 1 au no 17 d'Amerindia. Paris: Association d'Ethnolinguistique Amérindienne (A.E.A.). 148 pp.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 'Eléments de phonologie bahuana', §2.7 'La syllabe et l'accent tonique', point 3, pp. 25-26 (PDF pages 35-36); earlier phonetic statement p. 12 (PDF 22): 'La syllabe phonétique obéit donc à la formule : (C)V, et l'accent tonique tombe sur l'avant-dernière syllabe.'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the (fully affixed) phonological word, with the stressed vowel usually lengthened; underlying final vowels deleted in fast speech (leaving a final glottal stop) do not shift the stress, so such surface forms appear final-stressed; diphthongs are analysed as two syllables so that penultimate counting holds; stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'L'accent secondaire tombe deux syllabes avant l'accent primaire' (p. 25): secondary stress two syllables before the primary, i.e. alternating trochaic rhythm leftwards from the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Les exceptions à la règle sont rares' (p. 26): kiba [ki:ba] 'montagne', kibada [ki:bada] 'pierre' (initial stress with long vowel). Words ending in a glottal stop from fast-speech loss of the final vowel (mana' 'palmier sp.', winitsɨ' 'nourriture') are stressed on the surface-final syllable; slower speech restores the vowel (mana'a). Four or five words with kw/sw clusters too rare to analyse.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'L'accent touche le mot en sa totalité, quels que soient les affixes associés' (verb with 1-3 suffixes keeps penultimate stress: [ɸɨkaˈruta], [ɸɨkaruˈtana], [ɸɨkarutañaˈrɨna]). Data elicited June-August 1991 from a single, very elderly last speaker (Claudina de Souza Soares), partly in hospital; author warns of pronunciation instability (p. 9, 26). Stress marked by underlining in transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Ramirez 1992 describes 'Bahuana' as spoken by the last speaker, Claudina de Souza Soares, from the Shiriana/Ciriana village of the Demini (her late husband was the last Bahuana); he states that bahuana and ciriana are 'les deux aspects d'une seule et même langue' (p. 2) with 97% shared vocabulary (p. 5). Glottolog xiri1243 'Xiriâna' lists Bahuana, Chiriana, Shiriana as alternative names, so the source matches the target languoid exactly. Not to be confused with the Yanomaman 'Shiriana/Xiriana' (Ninam, nina1238), which Ramirez explicitly separates (2001: 511).

sources.note: §8.1 'Os Bahuana', pp. 511-514 (PDF 521-524): history, consonant/vowel inventory, neutralizations, elision/fusion rules, sound correspondences, person-affix sketch. No statement on stress for Bahuana; says Ramirez 1992 (two months with the last speaker) is the only study and the language is now extinct.
